Preparing to Teach | Spring 2026

A key part of teacher-research is preparing with intention: looking closely at the materials, anticipating how your students might respond, and beginning to name the questions you want to pay attention to as you teach. The steps and discussion below will guide you into that preparation work so you feel grounded before beginning the lesson sequence.

Below you will find the full Layered Writing Teacher Guide for this lesson sequence. Notice that the teacher guide also includes a Layered Writing Student-Facing Slideshow that you can copy and adapt for your classroom.

Choose a Text Set

The Layered Writing lesson sequence features five set options. The first step in preparing to teach the lesson sequence is to select the text set you will use with your students.

Consider the following questions as a guide for your decision:

  • Which topics will be most interesting to your students?

  • Which text set provides opportunities that best meet the needs of your learners?

  • Which text sets are more accessible to your learners?

To get started, take some time to explore the full text set for each option (linked in the teacher guide). You don't necessarily need to do a close reading of every single text in each text set option at this point, but it would be helpful to open and preview each text to get a sense of the format, length, vocabulary, level of complexity, etc.

One other note to consider as you are choosing a topic. Sometimes teachers feel like they need to avoid selecting text set topics that their students are unfamiliar with. However, in NWP's experience with text sets in the College, Career, and Community Writer's Program (C3WP), teachers often found that the text set topics their students didn't know much (or anything about) provided the highest engagement. So, keep that in mind when you are thinking about which topic you might choose.

Close Reading of Lesson Sequence

Once you have chosen your text set topic, the next step in preparing to teach is to do a close reading of the Layered Writing Lesson Teacher Guide.

As you read the lesson sequence, make note of

  • Number of suggested lessons and overall pacing

  • Resources and copies to prepare

  • Student skills/conceptual understandings

  • Connections to your curriculum and/or assessment standards

  • Important or tricky teacher moves

  • Experiences/learning activities that your students will enjoy and find motivating

  • Anything that seems like it might be challenging for your students

Click here to make your own copy of this teacher guide.


💬Reflect and Share

Now that you have taken some time to choose a text set and to look closely at the lesson sequence, go to the Preparing to Teach Discussionto share what you discovered.

Reflect on the following:

  • Which text set did you choose and why?

  • What are you looking forward to in teaching this lesson sequence?

  • What might be challenging, for you and/or your students?

  • What adaptations or adjustments do you think you might need to make?

  • Other questions or ideas

Be sure to take a few minutes to respond to at least two other teachers’ posts to continue the conversation.

Once you’ve posted and responded here, move on to the second discussion, where you’ll reflect on your experience during teaching the lesson sequence.

I am going to use the Teens and Technology text set with my 8th graders because it is so relevant to them. Cell phones were banned in schools in MO this year and I've heard mixed feedback. I want to relate this to the book we are beginning, Animal Farm. I think that I can tie in to reliability of information and people who might have something to gain from persuading others. I think that having them watch for both supporting and contradictory messages will prepare them for Animal Farm. I think that the stamina needed for the book will be challenging. If I can get them to go through the articles, then it should set them up for the thinking. But the weeks of connected thinking will be challenging. I plan on creating a guided annotation sheet to go with our layers that will act as their weekly comprehension work, but also a note catcher for our final written piece. I will also have an anchor chart of characters' actions. I wonder how the students will do with so many things going on. This layered work will be during my mini lessons and the more writing standard focused writing will be in small group writing. I wonder how I can facilitate understanding with so much going on. My plan is to use the mini lesson to gather information and the writing group to plan, write, and practice grammar through editing. My concern is time constraints.

Leigh A Rogers
9:09 pm

Planning my class text set was super exciting and felt immediately relevant to what I was trying to do in my Shakespeare unit. I decided to break away from the text sets offered so that mine would fit a bit better around the Julius Caesar excerpts we were getting ready to read in class. Within this unit, students are reading Shakespeare excerpts while reading independent reading books. The overall purpose in the unit is to choose a subject developing in a Shakespeare text and explore how that subject also developed in their independent reading books, then build synthesis thesis statements about them. In order to really expand the conversation, I decided to incorporate additional texts touching base on the subjects students were seeing so that they could form their thesis statements based on much larger conversations.

For Julius Caesar, I was able to focus the big subject around political polarization. In the same way Brutus felt his very violent path was the only way forward with Caesar, I wanted students to examine how a similar conversation is happening in our society today where political parties are shown as more obstinate in their stances, more likely to see the opposing side as morally wrong, and less likely to reach across the aisle. With that being said, I used the Layered Writing Powerpoint to include three different texts that all agreed American politics were very divided but texts that also offered very different solutions for how to fix that division. It was really important to me to pick neutral texts that didn't push students to the left or the right but rather focused on different approaches for bringing these two sides back together to be able to have more cohesive communities. A big thank you to Rachel for helping me get my last text to make these tie together nicely! You can see my three texts on this powerpoint: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1MVv5LMQuif7Tp8WRb-CuPchJifwRZFt3X3DA9nnOEnY/edit?usp=sharing. The two articles we worked with are in the speaker notes.

I was most looking forward to these texts bringing Julius Caesar to the forefront of why the text still matters today. So often, I feel like it's difficult to touch base on events unfolding today because I don't want to be accused of leaning to one side, I don't always know how to bring in all the voices of the conversation accurately, and sometimes, because of iterative journalism, it's hard to keep up with the developing conversation. However, this is where our students' passion lies. They want to talk about the world around them, they want to make sense of it, and they want to do that in a space where they can feel safe and not shut out. I was so excited to do that in a neutral way and show kids that we can have productive and informative questions without resorting to our echo chambers.

As far as challenges, I was most concerned about students trying to take the conversation in a political, "my-side" direction and losing focus in the class. For this reason, I felt it was essential to have timed partner discussions and really stress what the claim was before setting them off to start talking with their partners.

I chose the text set of Teens and Technology. I chose this because I feel like my 8th grade students would be the most interested in this topic. Before the law of no cell phones was passed, we always had a strict policy on no phones in our building... "Away for the Day." So, our students have gotten use to not being able to have their phones during school hours. However, one thing that has changed, is we can no longer allow them to take their phones on field trips. We hear a lot "my parents won't let me go without my phone." And we are finding that students are less likely to participate without their phones. I chose the article in this text set of "Yes, Teens Are Glued to Their Screens, But Here's What We're Missing." I am looking forward to teaching this and using this article because I feel it isn't completely downing teens using their phones but using a different approach to defend them as well as talk about necessary and doable approaches to lessening their screen time. I think the biggest challenge will be their mind set. Teens do not like to be told that they are on their phones too much so I think right away they will have the mind set of not wanting to read this but I am hopeful the title of the article will help them be more interested. I think it will give them a different perspective to discuss and allow for more of a debate.

Leigh A Rogers

Planning my class text set was super exciting and felt immediately relevant to what I was trying to do in my Shakespeare unit. I decided to break away from the text sets offered so that mine would fit a bit better around the Julius Caesar excerpts we were getting ready to read in class. Within this unit, students are reading Shakespeare excerpts while reading independent reading books. The overall purpose in the unit is to choose a subject developing in a Shakespeare text and explore how that subject also developed in their independent reading books, then build synthesis thesis statements about them. In order to really expand the conversation, I decided to incorporate additional texts touching base on the subjects students were seeing so that they could form their thesis statements based on much larger conversations.

For Julius Caesar, I was able to focus the big subject around political polarization. In the same way Brutus felt his very violent path was the only way forward with Caesar, I wanted students to examine how a similar conversation is happening in our society today where political parties are shown as more obstinate in their stances, more likely to see the opposing side as morally wrong, and less likely to reach across the aisle. With that being said, I used the Layered Writing Powerpoint to include three different texts that all agreed American politics were very divided but texts that also offered very different solutions for how to fix that division. It was really important to me to pick neutral texts that didn't push students to the left or the right but rather focused on different approaches for bringing these two sides back together to be able to have more cohesive communities. A big thank you to Rachel for helping me get my last text to make these tie together nicely! You can see my three texts on this powerpoint: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1MVv5LMQuif7Tp8WRb-CuPchJifwRZFt3X3DA9nnOEnY/edit?usp=sharing. The two articles we worked with are in the speaker notes.

I was most looking forward to these texts bringing Julius Caesar to the forefront of why the text still matters today. So often, I feel like it's difficult to touch base on events unfolding today because I don't want to be accused of leaning to one side, I don't always know how to bring in all the voices of the conversation accurately, and sometimes, because of iterative journalism, it's hard to keep up with the developing conversation. However, this is where our students' passion lies. They want to talk about the world around them, they want to make sense of it, and they want to do that in a space where they can feel safe and not shut out. I was so excited to do that in a neutral way and show kids that we can have productive and informative questions without resorting to our echo chambers.

As far as challenges, I was most concerned about students trying to take the conversation in a political, "my-side" direction and losing focus in the class. For this reason, I felt it was essential to have timed partner discussions and really stress what the claim was before setting them off to start talking with their partners.

How fantastic! I love how you've made the connection between past political party beliefs and today's political beliefs. I can imagine that this really stuck with your students and kept them engaged.

1. What are you looking forward to in teaching this lesson sequence?

I’m looking forward to students connecting this topic to their own lives. The question “Does school start too early?” is something they experience every day, so it’s highly engaging and relevant. Students will likely have strong opinions. I’m also excited for students to explore real evidence and research.

2. What might be challenging, for you and/or your students?

One challenge may be helping students understand that this issue is complex, not just “early = bad, later = good.” The article explains that while later start times may help with sleep, they also create problems like transportation issues, after-school scheduling conflicts, and family challenges .

Students might also struggle with: Understanding multiple perspectives (students vs. parents vs. schools), interpreting research and statistics, and avoiding overly simple arguments

For me as the teacher, it may be challenging to guide students to balance opinion with evidence instead of just sharing personal experiences.

3. What adaptations or adjustments might you need to make?

I may need to: Break the article into smaller sections so it’s easier for 7th graders to understand, pre-teach key vocabulary, provide graphic organizers

I might also include: a short discussion or poll about their own sleep habits

4. Other questions or ideas

Some ideas I’d like to explore: Would later start times actually make students go to bed earlier—or just stay up later? (a concern raised in the article)

I could also extend the lesson by having students: conduct a class survey on sleep habits or write a persuasive letter to the school board

Which text set did you choose and why?

I would select the Daylight Saving Time text set because it connects scientific concepts to students’ everyday lives in a way that is immediately relevant. Students experience time changes directly, especially through sleep disruptions, mood shifts, and changes in daily routines, which makes the topic engaging and meaningful. This text set also allows students to explore real-world science topics such as circadian rhythms, human biology, and the impact of environmental changes on the body. Additionally, it presents multiple perspectives; informational, health-related, and practical, which supports critical thinking and helps students understand that scientific issues are often complex rather than one-sided.

What are you looking forward to in teaching this lesson sequence?

I’m really looking forward to seeing how students’ thinking evolves over time. In science, students often want a “right answer,” so this approach; where they explore multiple perspectives before forming a claim, feels especially valuable. I think the visual mapping of the conversation will be a powerful moment, helping students see how scientific ideas and real-world issues connect. I’m also excited about the consistent, low-stakes writing because it gives all students a chance to process their thinking, not just the ones who are quick to speak up.

What might be challenging, for you and/or your students?

One challenge will be helping students feel comfortable without immediately choosing a side. Many of my students are used to forming quick opinions, so slowing down and revising their thinking may feel unfamiliar or even frustrating. Another challenge could be managing time, especially with meaningful discussions and writing layered across several days. For me, it may also be difficult to balance guidance with independence; knowing when to step in and when to let students wrestle with ideas.

What adaptations or adjustments do you think you might need to make?

I may need to scaffold the texts, especially for students who struggle with reading informational or health-related articles. This could include chunking the texts, pre-teaching key vocabulary, or offering guiding questions. I might also provide sentence starters or models for both discussion and writing to support students who need more structure. For the visual mapping, I may give a few concrete examples (like a simple Venn diagram or continuum) to help students get started. Additionally, I may adjust pacing; spending more time on discussion and mapping if students need it.

Other questions or ideas

I’m wondering how I can best assess student growth throughout the process, not just in the final argument. It might be helpful to track how their thinking changes from Day 1 to Day 4. I’m also thinking about how to connect this structure to future science units; this could be a great framework for topics like climate change, genetics, or human impact on ecosystems. Finally, I’d like to consider how to incorporate more student choice in topics down the line to increase engagement even further.

I really like how intentional your plan is, especially the connection between the Teens and Technology text set and Animal Farm, since focusing on reliability of information and persuasion creates a strong bridge into the novel’s themes of power and manipulation. Having students look for both supporting and contradictory messages is a great way to build the critical thinking they’ll need for analyzing characters’ influence, and using the articles as a “warm-up” for stamina is a smart approach. For time constraints, it may help to prioritize depth over coverage and use quick check-ins to monitor understanding without adding too much, and overall, your approach feels well-aligned and engaging, especially in how it makes the themes of Animal Farm relevant to students’ real-world experiences.

I chose to have my students read, write, and discuss the use of AI. Since

AI is not going anywhere, I feel a professional responsibility to teach students to use AI responsibly. I believe that AI is going to change the way teachers assign writing. In my college comp classes, we define an essay as "an attempt," and we define literacy as to "make meaning." Therefore, an essay is an attempt to make meaning out of our learning, which requires reflection. Since AI can write the classic five-paragraph essay better than most humans can, it is my belief that instructors must use writing as a way to help students synthesize their learning and thoughts in a way that allows them to attempt to make meaning. I think my students will worry about finding the "right" answer in this exercise; in other words, I think they will try to give the answer they think I want to hear.

Amanda Sampsel

1. What are you looking forward to in teaching this lesson sequence?

I’m looking forward to students connecting this topic to their own lives. The question “Does school start too early?” is something they experience every day, so it’s highly engaging and relevant. Students will likely have strong opinions. I’m also excited for students to explore real evidence and research.

2. What might be challenging, for you and/or your students?

One challenge may be helping students understand that this issue is complex, not just “early = bad, later = good.” The article explains that while later start times may help with sleep, they also create problems like transportation issues, after-school scheduling conflicts, and family challenges .

Students might also struggle with: Understanding multiple perspectives (students vs. parents vs. schools), interpreting research and statistics, and avoiding overly simple arguments

For me as the teacher, it may be challenging to guide students to balance opinion with evidence instead of just sharing personal experiences.

3. What adaptations or adjustments might you need to make?

I may need to: Break the article into smaller sections so it’s easier for 7th graders to understand, pre-teach key vocabulary, provide graphic organizers

I might also include: a short discussion or poll about their own sleep habits

4. Other questions or ideas

Some ideas I’d like to explore: Would later start times actually make students go to bed earlier—or just stay up later? (a concern raised in the article)

I could also extend the lesson by having students: conduct a class survey on sleep habits or write a persuasive letter to the school board

I chose to use this as one of my topics as well. It is something my students have had opinions on already this year because our district is transitioning to a 4-day week next year and students will have to start their day 20 mins earlier. There has been some class discussion on this. I'm glad to be able to pull in some research and let them see varying perspectives on the issue and that, as you said, it is not just "early=bad, later=good" and why.

Planning my class text set was super exciting and felt immediately relevant to what I was trying to do in my Shakespeare unit. I decided to break away from the text sets offered so that mine would fit a bit better around the Julius Caesar excerpts we were getting ready to read in class. Within this unit, students are reading Shakespeare excerpts while reading independent reading books. The overall purpose in the unit is to choose a subject developing in a Shakespeare text and explore how that subject also developed in their independent reading books, then build synthesis thesis statements about them. In order to really expand the conversation, I decided to incorporate additional texts touching base on the subjects students were seeing so that they could form their thesis statements based on much larger conversations.

For Julius Caesar, I was able to focus the big subject around political polarization. In the same way Brutus felt his very violent path was the only way forward with Caesar, I wanted students to examine how a similar conversation is happening in our society today where political parties are shown as more obstinate in their stances, more likely to see the opposing side as morally wrong, and less likely to reach across the aisle. With that being said, I used the Layered Writing Powerpoint to include three different texts that all agreed American politics were very divided but texts that also offered very different solutions for how to fix that division. It was really important to me to pick neutral texts that didn't push students to the left or the right but rather focused on different approaches for bringing these two sides back together to be able to have more cohesive communities. A big thank you to Rachel for helping me get my last text to make these tie together nicely! You can see my three texts on this powerpoint: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1MVv5LMQuif7Tp8WRb-CuPchJifwRZFt3X3DA9nnOEnY/edit?usp=sharing. The two articles we worked with are in the speaker notes.

I was most looking forward to these texts bringing Julius Caesar to the forefront of why the text still matters today. So often, I feel like it's difficult to touch base on events unfolding today because I don't want to be accused of leaning to one side, I don't always know how to bring in all the voices of the conversation accurately, and sometimes, because of iterative journalism, it's hard to keep up with the developing conversation. However, this is where our students' passion lies. They want to talk about the world around them, they want to make sense of it, and they want to do that in a space where they can feel safe and not shut out. I was so excited to do that in a neutral way and show kids that we can have productive and informative questions without resorting to our echo chambers.

As far as challenges, I was most concerned about students trying to take the conversation in a political, "my-side" direction and losing focus in the class. For this reason, I felt it was essential to have timed partner discussions and really stress what the claim was before setting them off to start talking with their partners.

I love what you are doing. It makes me feel better to know someone else is choosing a different text set than what is offered. I, too, chose a different text set to fit my needs. I love that you are doing this with Shakespeare. I used to teach high school, and Shakespeare can be so tricky. I wish I had had all these tools when I taught it. My son is learning Shakespeare right now, and he hates it because there are no engaging activities. He is told to read and answer questions. I hate that he is missing out on what could be a wonderful experience. Good Luck.

Amanda Sampsel

1. What are you looking forward to in teaching this lesson sequence?

I’m looking forward to students connecting this topic to their own lives. The question “Does school start too early?” is something they experience every day, so it’s highly engaging and relevant. Students will likely have strong opinions. I’m also excited for students to explore real evidence and research.

2. What might be challenging, for you and/or your students?

One challenge may be helping students understand that this issue is complex, not just “early = bad, later = good.” The article explains that while later start times may help with sleep, they also create problems like transportation issues, after-school scheduling conflicts, and family challenges .

Students might also struggle with: Understanding multiple perspectives (students vs. parents vs. schools), interpreting research and statistics, and avoiding overly simple arguments

For me as the teacher, it may be challenging to guide students to balance opinion with evidence instead of just sharing personal experiences.

3. What adaptations or adjustments might you need to make?

I may need to: Break the article into smaller sections so it’s easier for 7th graders to understand, pre-teach key vocabulary, provide graphic organizers

I might also include: a short discussion or poll about their own sleep habits

4. Other questions or ideas

Some ideas I’d like to explore: Would later start times actually make students go to bed earlier—or just stay up later? (a concern raised in the article)

I could also extend the lesson by having students: conduct a class survey on sleep habits or write a persuasive letter to the school board

First, I love how thoroughly you answered these questions. I can tell you really dove into the texts before committing to a topic, and I applaud that. I selfishly chose the topic I wanted to learn more about. I love your idea about the pre-teaching key vocabulary and I might even expand on it further to give even more background knowledge. I often find the students i have lack the life experiences to understand the context around a story, and the more relevant I can make it to them the higher the student engagement.

Which text set did you choose and why?

I would select the Daylight Saving Time text set because it connects scientific concepts to students’ everyday lives in a way that is immediately relevant. Students experience time changes directly, especially through sleep disruptions, mood shifts, and changes in daily routines, which makes the topic engaging and meaningful. This text set also allows students to explore real-world science topics such as circadian rhythms, human biology, and the impact of environmental changes on the body. Additionally, it presents multiple perspectives; informational, health-related, and practical, which supports critical thinking and helps students understand that scientific issues are often complex rather than one-sided.

What are you looking forward to in teaching this lesson sequence?

I’m really looking forward to seeing how students’ thinking evolves over time. In science, students often want a “right answer,” so this approach; where they explore multiple perspectives before forming a claim, feels especially valuable. I think the visual mapping of the conversation will be a powerful moment, helping students see how scientific ideas and real-world issues connect. I’m also excited about the consistent, low-stakes writing because it gives all students a chance to process their thinking, not just the ones who are quick to speak up.

What might be challenging, for you and/or your students?

One challenge will be helping students feel comfortable without immediately choosing a side. Many of my students are used to forming quick opinions, so slowing down and revising their thinking may feel unfamiliar or even frustrating. Another challenge could be managing time, especially with meaningful discussions and writing layered across several days. For me, it may also be difficult to balance guidance with independence; knowing when to step in and when to let students wrestle with ideas.

What adaptations or adjustments do you think you might need to make?

I may need to scaffold the texts, especially for students who struggle with reading informational or health-related articles. This could include chunking the texts, pre-teaching key vocabulary, or offering guiding questions. I might also provide sentence starters or models for both discussion and writing to support students who need more structure. For the visual mapping, I may give a few concrete examples (like a simple Venn diagram or continuum) to help students get started. Additionally, I may adjust pacing; spending more time on discussion and mapping if students need it.

Other questions or ideas

I’m wondering how I can best assess student growth throughout the process, not just in the final argument. It might be helpful to track how their thinking changes from Day 1 to Day 4. I’m also thinking about how to connect this structure to future science units; this could be a great framework for topics like climate change, genetics, or human impact on ecosystems. Finally, I’d like to consider how to incorporate more student choice in topics down the line to increase engagement even further.

I also think a huge challenge is students feeling comfortable without immediately choosing a side. I chose the school start time set, and I have a feeling most students will make up their minds after reading just the article titles. I'm hoping that through discussions, my students will look at multiple perspectives and evaluate them a bit before setting their opinions in stone.
